The answer is: ...were sitting by a fire they had made in the open, when one of them looked up and saw three strange forms in the sky. What are they? Are they good?

The reply is: The man who had been looking up at the sky said: "I do not know. Let us go home and ask the old people." So they went home, and they told the old people about the forms they had seen. The old people said: "Those are the spirits of our ancestors. They are good."
From that time on, every time the men of Egulac saw the forms in the sky they knew that it was their ancestors who were watching over them. And every time they went to hunt or to war, they saw the forms in the sky and knew that their ancestors were with them.
And the forms in the sky were always there. Some people said that they looked like people, only that they were made of clouds. Others said that they looked like birds, but that their wings were made of clouds.

But as they pulled away from the shore, they heard the drums start to beat again, and they knew that they would never again be safe from the vengeance of the Iroquoians.

Then they heard war-cries, and they thought: "Maybe this is a war-party". They escaped to the shore, and hid behind a log. Now canoes came up, and they heard the noise of paddles, and saw one canoe coming up to them. There were five men in the canoe, and they said: "What do you think? We wish to take you along. We are going up the river to make war on the people." One of the young men said,"I have no arrows." "Arrows are in the canoe," they said. "I will not go along. I might be killed. My relatives do not know where I have gone. But you," he said, turning to the other, "may go with them." So one of the young men went, but the other returned home. And the warriors went on up the river to a town on the other side of Kalama. The people came down to the water and they began to fight, and many were killed. But presently the young man heard one of the warriors say, "Quick, let us go home: that man has been hit." Now he thought: "Oh, they are ghosts." He did not feel sick, but they said he had been shot. So the canoes went back to Egulac and the young man went ashore to his house and made a fire. And he told everybody and said: "Behold I accompanied the ghosts, and we went to fight. Many of our fellows were killed, and many of those who attacked us were killed. They said I was hit, and I did not feel sick." He told it all, and then he became quiet. When the sun rose he fell down. Something black came out of his mouth. His face became contorted. The people jumped up and cried. He was dead.

What do we mean to the universe?" The other replied, "To the universe, my friend, we are but a few atoms. To each other, we mean everything."

Background
This is a Canadian Indian joke, or perhaps a Native American joke, as both groups have a tradition of telling such tales. The joke has been in circulation since at least 1975, and has been told and retold in many variations. It has been popularized through its inclusion in the book Native American Humor by Richard Gatlin (ISBN 0-87975-010-8), published by North Atlantic Books in 1995.

Analysis
The joke is an example of the "cosmic perspective" genre of humor, in which the vastness and emptiness of space are used to put human problems into perspective, and to remind the listener of his or her insignificance within the universe. It is also an example of the "two men" genre, a staple of joke-telling since at least the time of Aesop. The joke works best when told aloud, in a conversational style, with appropriate pauses for effect.

Variations
There are many variations of this joke. In some, the two men are said to be from the Cree tribe, or from the Saulteaux tribe, or from the Ojibway tribe, or from the Lakota tribe, or from the Comanche tribe, or from the Navajo tribe. In others, they are hunters, or fishermen, or astronauts, or alien visitors. Some variations include a punchline about how the universe doesn't care about us, or about how we are all connected, or about how we should live our lives to the fullest.

Egulac is a rural locality in Ontario, Canada, within the geographic township of Adelaide. It is situated 15 kilometres (9.3 mi) north of the municipality of Tillsonburg and 20 kilometres (12 mi) south of the city of London, along Highway 2. The name "Egulac" is derived from the Ojibwe language and means "place of the horned serpents".

History
The area was first explored by the French Canadian pioneer Jean Rousseaux, who established a fur trading post at the junction of the Thames and Miles rivers in 1818. The post was later moved to a site 1.6 kilometres (1 mi) up the Miles River, where the village of Egulac was later established. In 1824, Rousseaux sold the post to his neighbour, Nicholas Mastric. In 1849, Mastric sold the land to Edward P. Alford, who established a new post and named it after his hometown in England, Egulac.The village was incorporated in 1873 and became a municipality in 1908. It peaked in population in 1911, when it had 525 residents. The village then declined as people moved to more prosperous areas. In 1920, a fire destroyed much of the village, and it never recovered. The answer is: ...were sitting in a canoe facing the current watching the stars. One was Hare, the other Turtle. Hare said to Turtle, "I just dreamt that we were to go to the moon and I was to transform you into a rabbit." "And what are rabbits good for?" asked Turtle. "They are good for hunting and eating," replied Hare. "But we are not rabbits," said Turtle. "If we were, you would be the rabbit, not I." "That is true," said Hare, "but in my dream, you were a rabbit." "Let us go back to our village then," said Turtle. They paddled back to the village, and as they landed, Hare transformed himself into a rabbit and ran away. Turtle, who had not been transformed, was captured and eaten by the Iroquois.

Variants
This story is known in slightly different variations as "The Rabbit and the Turtle", "Hare and Turtle", or "The Two Friends". In some tellings, the transformations are permanent, in others they are not. In at least one variation, the roles of Hare and Turtle are reversed. In all variations, the moral is that one should not boast about one's abilities.

Origin
This story is found in the book "Legends of the Iroquois" by William J. Holland, first published in 1910. It is told as if it were a true story, passed down from generation to generation by the Iroquois people.

This is a line from the poem "The Raven" by Edgar Allan Poe. In the poem, the narrator is telling of how he was awoken by the sound of the raven tapping at his window, and how he descended into madness as the bird continued to perch and say "Nevermore." The line in question is from the second stanza, and is explaining that the narrator and another unnamed person were out hunting when they stumbled upon a spade, which led them to suspect fraud upon finding it inferred that the person who owned the spade must have also owned the place where they were hunting, and so the hunters concluded that they were being cheated out of their right to hunt on land they thought was open to them.
In this way, the line is employing a form of circular reasoning to create a sense of foreboding and mystery, as the narrator begins to believe that everything around him is part of a grand conspiracy to drive him to anger and despair. The overall effect is to create an atmosphere of gothic horror, in which the unknown is both terrifying and exciting to the audience.

Commentary
This folktale, acquired by Franz Boas from an unidentified egaleo informant c. 1890, has its basis in reality: Europeans unaccustomed to the stark weather conditions of the Canadian west could easily be caught off guard and overwhelmed by the power of the elements on the prairies. The tale also has antecedents in Western drama, specifically the genre known as Ship's Tale, or Nekomi Kishi monogatari, a popular form of Japanese folktale. In these tales, two men are trapped on a ship during a storm at sea, and one must remain behind to operate the ship's pump while the other seeks aid. The most famous example is in the short story "The Storm-Boy" (くроваすのㆍおもがたり, Kurozasu no omogataridori) by Ryunosuke Akutsushi. Furthermore, the man who stays behind in the egaleo tale is unharmed by the tempest, unlike in the Japanese short story where the man who remains behind is usually struck dead by a lightning bolt.

The men were cold, so they lit a fire in the cabin. They sat by the fire and played their guitars, singing sad songs about lost love. Suddenly, through the window, they saw a beautiful woman standing in the snow. She sang a song that was so beautiful that they were enchanted.
The men invited her to join them in the cabin and she agreed. They continued to play their guitars and sing, but the woman was silent. She just stood by the fire, staring into it.
After a while, one of the men spoke to her. Her name was Ada. She said that she was waiting for her lover, who was late coming home from the hunt. The men offered to help her look for him, but she refused, saying that he would come to her eventually.
They continued to play their guitars and sing, the woman joining in with them. The night passed quickly and before long, the first rays of the sun were coming through the window. Ada thanked the men for the wonderful evening and then left, disappearing into the forest.
The men returned to their own village, feeling that they had shared in an ancient tradition, an unforgettable night with a beautiful woman, a night that would stay with them forever.

The story
There was a time, he said, when the world was so covered with snow that no one could travel. The fire was small and weak, and the people huddled close to it for warmth. One day a man named Mish-Mish came to Ishkodag's village. He was a strange man, with red hair and a beard, and he wore furs that no one had ever seen before.
Mish-Mish told the people that he came from a far-off land, where the sun shone all the time, and the people never wore furs. He said that the world would never be covered in snow again, and that the fire would burn brightly.
Some of the people did not believe Mish-Mish, but Ishkodag's mother believed him. She went outside and danced around the fire, singing a song that meant "The sun is strong." The fire grew larger, and the people were warmed by it. Mish-Mish smiled, and then he disappeared.
From that day on, the world was never covered in snow again. The fire burned brightly, and the people wore fewer furs. Mish-Mish became a great chief, and his name was remembered for many generations.

The meaning of the story
The story of Mish-Mish is a creation myth, told to explain how the world came to be as it is. In the story, Mish-Mish represents the sun, which is the source of warmth and light

The answer is: ... came over to our camp. One was riding a white horse, the other a black horse. They wore their hair long, and were fully painted with black stripes over their eyes and noses, and their bodies were smeared with black paint from head to foot. They came to trade with us. We gave them some beads and other small gifts, and they gave us some white and black horses in return. They were very noisy and boisterous, and laughed a great deal.
From the book 'The Trail of the Sun-Dance Path' by Frank B. Sollie

Interpretation
This is a standard ethnographic description of a trade encounter between a European observer's camp and a group of Plains Indians. The two representatives of Egulac are described as painting themselves and wearing their hair long, which were marks of reverence and honor among the Plains people for those involved in sun-dance or other vision quests. The fact that they were riding white and black horses, the colors of the east and west directions, suggests that they were probably medicine men or war leaders. The fact that they gave the observer's camp white and black horses in return for trade goods indicates that they were highly respected and probably influential members of their own society as well. The author does not specify which group the men belonged to, but by the time the book was published in 1913, most of the Plains tribes had been displaced from their original territories and were living on reservations, where sun-dance and other traditional practices were severely restricted.

The origin of the tales of One Night Two Men comes from the first contact between Europeans and the indigenous people of the region. According to some versions, the "Two Men" were really Two Winnebagoes. In other stories, they are Dakota. In more violent tales, the "Two Men" kill each other at dawn, leaving the woman to grieve.Although the tale seems to endorse the superiority of white civilization, it can also be seen as a warning that white civilization will eventually fade away as well. Other interpretations emphasize the tragic elements of the tale, such as the idea of eternal conflict between those who have power and those who are oppressed.These tales were told and retold many times, each time with slight varitions. They heard the noise again, and this time they saw a bear. It turned out to be a large dog. The men belonged to the FNQIC (First Nations Technical Vocational College) Bear Club. They were there to trap bears for the fur trade. They had been drinking and had mistaken a dog for a bear.

History
The FNQIC Bear Club was founded in 1979 by Freddy J. Limogeau. It was one of several clubs that emerged from the broader Native American Bear Dance movement of the 1970s. The club was based at the FNQIC vocational college in Kashechewan, Ontario, and was affiliated with the Ontario Bear Federation. The club was active from 1979 to 1985, and was revived briefly in 1991. The club's purpose was to provide a legal outlet for native people to hunt bears, at a time when bear hunting was restricted by the Ontario government. The club obtained a bear hunting permit from the province, and also had a fur trading license. The club's presidency passed through three leaders: Freddy J. Limogeau, Joseph Merrill, and Tom Bouchard. In 1985, the club was shut down by the Ontario government, after a complaint was filed against it by the Ontario Wildlife Federation. The club was accused of exceeding its permitted quota of bears, and also of selling bear parts illegally. The club was revived in 1991, but was soon shut down again. In 1994, Limogeau was charged with offences related to the club's operations.

The answer is: ...came to a cabin in the woods. They heard a noise, and one of them said, "I bet it's a bear." The other said, "Bets are off."

Explanation
This is a setup for a joke. The punchline depends on the listener understanding that the speaker of the second line is saying "there's no bet" because he thinks the noise is not from a bear, but from something else (perhaps the owner of the cabin). Therefore, there would be no point in betting on it. The joke relies on a double entendre: "bets are off" can mean "there's no bet" (the usual meaning) and also "the betting is over" (a less common meaning).
The joke depends on the listener understanding that the first speaker is unlikely to believe that the noise is not from a bear, and so the second speaker's response is unexpected and humorous. The humor also comes from the form of the joke: it is in the form of a riddle, and the punchline is the answer to the riddle.

Origin
The joke has been told in many forms for decades, if not centuries. A similar joke has been told about two men who come across a woman in the woods at night. One man says, "She's probably a bear." "How can you tell?" the other man asks. "Well," the first man replies, "she has a bear-y of a face." The joke has been told in many cultures, including Native American cultures. The answer is: ...came to a cabin in the woods. They heard a noise, and one man said, "I bet it's a bear." The other man said, "Bears don't come here; there's a trap nearby." They heard the noise again, and this time they saw a bear. The first man said, "You said there was a trap?" The second man replied, "I said there was nearby."

The cabin in the woods is a metaphor for an uncertain situation. The two men represent two possible approaches to dealing with uncertainty: the first man insists on his initial interpretation (a bear) even when faced with contradictory evidence (the noise), while the second man is more flexible and open to revising his interpretation (a trap) when presented with new information. The moral of the story is that it is often better to keep an open mind and be prepared to revise one's beliefs in the face of new evidence.

Attribution
This story is often told as a Sufi parable, and appears in many collections of Sufi tales. It is also told in Hindu and Buddhist traditions, and has been adopted by the New Age movement. The version presented here is from the book "One Night Two Men" by William Benjamin K. The story has been retold many times, and has entered the public domain.

On 1 July 1884, two men from Egulac (a First Nations community on the Quebec-Ontario border) travelled to Verchuelen, Ontario, to participate in a treaty signng.  They were Tsenahree, an elder, and ABC, a young man.  There or perhaps on the trip itself they became intoxicated.  Some sources say that they were drunk on whiskey; others that they were drunk on pinty (a traditionally fermented Native American drink).  In any case, they were rowdy and disruptive at the treaty signing, which was taking place in a church.  They were told by the Indian agent to go outside.  Once outside, they were told by the agent to return to Egulac.  They didn't like this at all.  Tsenahree was particularly angry, and he made threats against the agent.  The agent backed down, and permitted the two men to stay.  After some time, Tsenahree and ABC departed, and returned to their community.  However, only soon after arriving home, Tsenahree died.  It is unclear whether his death was natural, or occurred as a result of his intoxication.

This event is narrated in William Lewis Tougée's classic work, "The Treaties of Canada With The Indians of Manitoba and The North-West Territories Including The Negotiations on Which They Were Based, and Other Information Relating Thereto" (1886).

The poem does not say which man Emily was in love with, or even if she loved either of them. The poem ends with the line "But Emily slept the sleep of guiltless dreams,/And the morrow bore no tale of woes" which suggests that whatever happened that night, Emily was not harmed by it.

Sir John Sparrow David Thompson,  (November 10, 1845 – December 12, 1894) was a Canadian lawyer, judge and politician who served as the fourth prime minister of Canada from 1892 until his death.

Early life and education
Born in Halifax, Nova Scotia, Thompson was of Irish descent. He studied law and was called to the bar in 1865.

Career
Thompson became a Queen's Counsel in 1878, and was elected to the House of Commons that year. He was reelected in 1882, 1887, and 1891. Thompson was appointed to the Supreme Court of Canada in 1888, and was sworn in as a member of the privy council. In 1891, he became the fourth prime minister of Canada, following the death of John Abbott. He was the first Roman Catholic to hold the position. On a trip to England in 1894, Thompson unexpectedly suffered a heart attack and died, aged 49. He is the second and most recent Canadian prime minister to have died in office, after John A. Macdonald.

Legacy
Thompson is the only Roman Catholic prime minister Canada has had to date. During his brief tenure, he sought to expand the use of electricity and railway systems throughout the country, and worked to establish a unique Canadian identity separate from both Great Britain and the United States. Notably, he established the Canadian Mounted Police and the Immigration and Colonization Offices.
In 1967, Thompson was named to the Canadian Hall of Fame. In 1997, he was designated a Persons of National Historic Significance. In 2004, he was honoured by being placed on the $20 banknote.

The song "One Night Two Men"  is a traditional English broadside ballad which has been performed by the Canadian folk group, The Cody Ceilidh. The song tells the story of two men who meet in a tavern and boast of their exploits. One is an English highwayman, the other is a Canadian Mountie. One night two Malays were gambling at a farm owned by an Orang Asli. The couple who lived there kept the couple Company. What happened (in detail)? The answer is: The gamblers were angry when they lost all their money and began to insult the wife of the owner of the farm. They grabbed their guns and left, threatening to return with others to "teach them a lesseron". The couple knew they could rely on the village militia for protection, but the gamblers returned with a large posse of other men and attacked the village, burning houses and killing people. The couple managed to escape, but the owners of the farm were killed by the rampaging crowd. The couple walked to a nearby Dutch fort and were protected there for some hours. Then a messenger came from the Resident of the District, begging the Dutch to return the couple to their village, as they were the only witnesses to the crime. The Dutch insisted that the Resident make a written promise that the couple would not be harmed before they were returned. Even though the Resident wrote the promise, as soon as the couple arrived in the village, they were attacked and killed by the crowd. The Orang Asli were fully integrated into Malayan society, although they retained some of their own customs and beliefs. They were proud of their malayanidentity and sought to perpetuate it by teaching their children the Malay language and customs.

Found near the village of Squamish in what is now British Columbia, Canada, the basic story was first published in English by Carrickcroft Press in 1914. It was later published in both French and German translations. The novel was expanded into a full-length work titled "The Adventures of Two Men from Egulac" and republished in 1920. The tale has been subsequently retold many times,including being illustrated by Leigh Brackett and retold as a children's story in 1958, and retold again in French in 1966. The original title of "One Night" has led to widespread confusion, and the numerous retellings have evolved into distinct stories, some with significantly different plots.
In all versions, the two men are from Egulac (a misspelling of Halkumax, a local First Nations tribe), and are renowned for their strength and bravery. In the original story, they are invited to a potlatch hosted by a neighbouring tribe, but offend the host by laughing at his attempting to steal one of their magic bowls. As punishment, the hosts decide to pull apart the pair with giant spruce trees. Just before this happens, however, a wise woman suggests that a test of strength should decide the outcome of the dispute, and the host agrees. The two men grasp hands and pull mightily, and are pulled apart, the trees missing the pair by only a few feet. The host then offers his daughter in marriage to one of the men, and they depart in peace.

In Heath's illustration, the hermit is seen feeding the duckling bread crumbs while the pool is surrounded by green plants. One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then they heard war-cries, and they thought: "Maybe this is a war-party". They escaped to the shore, and hid behind a log. Now canoes came up, and they heard the noise of paddles, and saw one canoe coming up to them. There were five men in the canoe, and they said: "What do you think? We wish to take you along. We are going up the river to make war on the Kamloopss." One of the younger men said,"I'm from Ekalaka, from the country of the Pikuni (Arrow-children), my father's an elder and my mother's a sister of the Emperor." The other young man said, "I'm from Starry River, from the country of the Minook (Papoose)." Then the elder said, "Walook, Walook!" —That means "Walk, walk!" in their language. "Walk upon the beach and look around." They walked around and looked, and saw many marine otter-skins, and some men lying in the Waterproof Canoe. "'Go ahead,' said the captain of the canoe, "we have killed eight moose that are hanging up there." One of the young men said, "I'm ashamed of you; that you treat your enemies in such a way." Then one of the men from Starry River said, "My father talks often here. He said that when we grow up we shall get such a canoe, and put our names on it." Then the young men came in with the five, and they got into the Waterproof Canoe with the others, and padded up to where the mooses were hanging, and they had supper there.
